solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Body politic, say

definitions.meaning: a nation considered as one organised political body

definitions.note: a verb, while the other definition is a noun
definitions.meaning: to say something formally is to declare it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' looks like the usual crossword signal for an example, but here it is a second definition: to STATE is to say.
explanation.definitionFit: A nation or commonwealth is the organised political community, and to declare something plainly is the verb sense.

clue.text: Fat woman on top of tram

indicators.note: in a down clue, 'on top of' places the woman's name above the letter taken from the vehicle

parts.note: a common girl's name standing for any woman

indicators.note: the top of a word written downwards is its opening letter, so only the tram's first letter is used

parts.note: the opening letter of the vehicle

explanation.surface: An unkind picture of a large woman riding on the upper deck of a tram.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fat' reads as an adjective describing the woman, but it is the noun definition standing apart from the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Suet is the hard animal fat from around the kidneys, used in British puddings and pastry.

clue.text: A mother? He didn't have one!

definitions.text: A mother? He didn't have one!

parts.note: the article used as it stands
the word breeders use for the female parent of a foal or calf

explanation.surface: A quizzical exchange about someone who never had a mother at all.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: in Genesis the first man was made from dust, so he was the one person with no mother.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Bible story the first man was created directly by God, so he alone was never born to anyone.

clue.text: Pet reason for developing an artificial language

indicators.note: something developing changes its form, so the letters of the first two words are rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: Someone's favourite motive for inventing a new language of their own.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pet' looks like an adjective meaning favourite, but both words are simply letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Esperanto was invented by Zamenhof in the 1880s as a constructed international tongue, the best-known one.

clue.text: Wine greeting worker in Channel Islands

indicators.note: things put in the islands sit between their two abbreviated letters

parts.note: the standard abbreviation for the islands, split to hold the rest
an informal hello
the worker ant is the usual crossword worker

explanation.surface: A wine served as a welcome to someone who works on Jersey or Guernsey.
explanation.walkthrough: The Channel Islands (Jersey, Guernsey and their neighbours) abbreviate to CI; the hello and the ant go between those two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Chianti is the famous red from Tuscany, traditionally sold in straw-covered bottles.

clue.text: Inexpensive old banger impounded by commanding officer

indicators.note: a car impounded is locked inside, so the old banger goes inside the officer's letters

parts.note: the usual abbreviation for a commanding officer
a banger is British slang for a battered old car, and so is a heap

explanation.surface: The commanding officer confiscates a cheap wreck of a car.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a banger is a sausage but also a clapped-out car; a heap is another word for that car.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheapo is informal slang for something low-priced and of poor quality, costing little money.

clue.text: Unspecified doctrine originally inspiring so many

indicators.note: what comes originally is at the start, so each of the following words gives its first letter

parts.note: the opening letters of the three words

explanation.surface: A vague belief that once inspired a great many followers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unspecified' is fair because the answer is the suffix used on its own for any doctrine not named.
explanation.definitionFit: An ism is informally any belief system or ideology, the suffix of communism, socialism and the rest used alone.

clue.text: Idea about army musicians method of writing

indicators.note: the idea goes round, or about, the army's abbreviation

parts.note: a notion is an idea
the Territorial Army, Britain's volunteer reserve

explanation.surface: Thoughts about military bandsmen and how they write things down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Army musicians' reads as a single phrase, a military band, but the split falls between them: 'army' is wordplay and 'musicians' begins the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Musical notation is the system of staves, clefs and symbols in which players record and read music.

clue.text: Relaxed boy attending class first

indicators.note: 'first' puts the phrase for attending class ahead of the boy's name

parts.note: a pupil attending class is in their form, the British word for a school class
a short boy's name

explanation.surface: A laid-back boy who has turned up to lessons early.
explanation.walkthrough: In British schools a form is a class or year group, so attending class is being in form.
explanation.definitionFit: Casual and unofficial manners or dress are relaxed, without ceremony or strict rules.

clue.text: Instance of former politician overwhelmed by drink

parts.note: an ex is a former one

indicators.note: something overwhelmed by drink is swamped, surrounded by it, so the politician sits inside

parts.note: beer, split around the politician
a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A case of an ex-politician who has had far too much to drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Former politician' reads as one person, but 'former' supplies its own chunk at the front while the politician goes into the ale.
explanation.definitionFit: An example is a single case or specimen illustrating a general rule, which is what an instance is.

clue.text: Doctor rejected attack — a distinctive idea

parts.note: a medical officer

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the word for attack is written backwards

parts.note: a fit of coughing or temper is an attack

explanation.surface: A medic turns down an assault, with a pointed comment about a distinctive idea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Attack' suggests violence, but here it is an attack of illness, a fit.
explanation.definitionFit: A motif is a recurring theme or design element in art, music or literature, a characteristic idea.

clue.text: Appropriate legwear, reportedly, for one spreading the message?

indicators.note: what is reported is heard rather than seen, so the two words are said out loud

parts.note: proper means appropriate, and a gaiter is a covering for the lower leg

explanation.surface: Asks what the correct trousers or leggings would be for someone evangelising.
explanation.walkthrough: A gaiter is a cloth or leather covering for the ankle and shin; 'proper gaiter' said quickly gives PROPAGATOR.
explanation.definitionFit: To propagate a belief or idea is to spread it widely, so a propagator broadcasts the word.

clue.text: Senior relative finally fuming about a gibe

indicators.note: what comes finally is at the end, so only the closing letter of the next word is used

parts.note: the closing letter of the angry word
re means about or concerning
the article used as it stands
a jeering remark

explanation.surface: An elderly relative seething over some insult.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like a container indicator, but here it is simply RE, as in a memo heading.
explanation.definitionFit: A great-aunt is the sister of a grandparent, a family member from an older generation.

clue.text: Information secured by factory — it makes us mournful

definitions.note: a phrase describing a sound; the answer is an adjective

indicators.note: what is secured by the factory is held within it, so the information goes inside

parts.note: a manufacturing plant
gen is British slang for information

explanation.surface: Secret data locked up at a works, and something sad about it.
explanation.walkthrough: Gen is informal British for information, as in 'get the gen'. The definition is loose: a plangent sound is one that makes the listener sad.
explanation.definitionFit: Plangent describes a loud, resonant sound with a melancholy, plaintive quality, such as a tolling bell.

clue.text: Distant object, something of negligible value once

parts.note: far away
an object is a thing

explanation.surface: A faraway object, perhaps a star, that once seemed worthless.
explanation.walkthrough: A farthing was an old British coin worth a quarter of a penny, withdrawn in 1961; 'once' flags that it no longer exists.
explanation.definitionFit: The coin was the smallest British denomination, so 'not worth a farthing' meant nearly worthless.

clue.text: Studied art mostly in period of abstinence

indicators.note: 'mostly' keeps most of the word for art and drops its final letter
the shortened art is placed in the period of abstinence

parts.note: the forty days before Easter when Christians give things up
art without its last letter

explanation.surface: Someone did most of their art studies while giving things up for Lent.
explanation.walkthrough: The spelling with -t is the usual British past tense, where Americans write learned.
explanation.definitionFit: Having studied something means having acquired knowledge of it, the past tense of the verb learn.

clue.text: Iron Lady's felt hat

parts.note: the chemical symbol for iron
a woman's name standing for any lady

explanation.surface: Margaret Thatcher, nicknamed the Iron Lady, and her felt hat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Iron Lady' reads as Thatcher's nickname, but it splits into the symbol for iron and a woman's name; 'felt' is the fabric, not the past tense of feel.
explanation.definitionFit: A fedora is a soft brimmed hat with a creased crown, traditionally made of felt.

clue.text: Line up outside initially under coercion

indicators.note: the word for line up sits outside, wrapping round the letter taken from the next word

parts.note: soldiers dress ranks when they line up straight

indicators.note: what comes initially is at the start, so only the opening letter of 'under' is used

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: People forced to queue outside under threat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Under coercion' reads as one phrase, but 'under' is wordplay and 'coercion' alone is the definition. To dress is a military term for lining troops up.
explanation.definitionFit: Duress is compulsion by threats or force, pressure making someone act against their will.

clue.text: Toys, donuts, being flogged? That's fairly good

indicators.note: things being flogged are beaten about, so the letters of the toys and donuts are knocked into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: Toys and doughnuts on sale, and someone reckons that is a decent deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flogged' is British slang for sold as well as beaten, which is what makes the surface read naturally. 'Not so dusty' is a British idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: The British idiom means reasonably good or not bad at all, a mild understated compliment.

clue.text: Mediocre journalist's horse

definitions.meaning: a writer churning out dull copy for pay
a horse for ordinary riding, or one hired out

explanation.surface: The horse belonging to an undistinguished reporter.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive makes it look like one thing owned by the other, but it only joins two separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses come from hackney, a hired riding horse, and hence a writer hired to do drudge work.

clue.text: River to north of Cambs city bank?

indicators.note: in a down clue the northern piece is written above, so the river's letter comes before the city

parts.note: the map abbreviation for river
the cathedral city in Cambridgeshire (Cambs)

explanation.surface: Points to a riverbank just north of a city in Cambridgeshire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bank' wants to be a river bank, fitting the surface, but it is the verb, as in bank on someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To bank on someone is to depend on or trust them, the same as relying.

clue.text: Musical entertainment viewed in the Adelphi originally?

indicators.note: what comes originally is at the start, so the words before it give their opening letters

parts.note: the opening letters of the five words

explanation.surface: A musical show seen at the Adelphi, a theatre in London's West End.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Musical entertainment' reads as the definition, but 'entertainment' starts the letter run. The question mark admits the show did not in fact open at the Adelphi.
explanation.definitionFit: Evita is the Lloyd Webber and Rice stage show about Eva Perón, wife of Argentina's president.

clue.text: A couple of points engendering reverential fear

parts.note: the article used as it stands
two compass points, west and east

explanation.surface: Two remarks that leave listeners in wonder.
explanation.walkthrough: Points in crosswords are usually compass points; here two of them sit side by side after the A.
explanation.definitionFit: Awe is wonder mixed with dread or respect, as felt before something vast or holy.

clue.text: Copy flightless bird no longer living

parts.note: the large Australian bird that cannot fly
the late someone is dead

explanation.surface: Imitating a flightless bird that has gone extinct, like the dodo.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points to the dodo, but the bird is the crossword's favourite three-letter one.
explanation.definitionFit: To emulate someone is to imitate them, trying to match or equal their achievements.

clue.text: Worried sister nursing head of 11's big cat

indicators.note: something worried is agitated, so the letters of the sister are stirred up with the added one
to nurse is to hold close, so the sister takes in the extra letter before being mixed

parts.note: anagram fodder, six letters

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, so only the start of 11 down is used

parts.note: the first letter of the answer to 11 down

explanation.surface: An anxious sister caring for a relative's big cat.
explanation.walkthrough: The sister is used letter for letter, not as SIS or NUN; with the first letter of GREAT-AUNT added, the seven letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A tigress is a female tiger, one of the large wild felines.

clue.text: Wine from Hungary, ultimately just right

indicators.note: what comes ultimately is at the end, so only the closing letter of 'just' is used

parts.note: the closing letter of the word
right as in all right or fine

explanation.surface: A Hungarian wine that is, in the end, just right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ultimately' looks as if it belongs to Hungary, but it acts on the word after it: the last letter of 'just'.
explanation.definitionFit: Tokay, or Tokaji, is the sweet dessert wine from the Tokaj region of northeastern Hungary.
